function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run manually).  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to the repo for you, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

> The repo is a very small Node.js “Hello World” style app.  
> It contains a `package.json`, an `app.js` that listens on port **3000**, and a `README.md`.  
> No Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests or CI workflow exist yet.

### 2.1 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this image?*  
> `node:18-alpine` is small, stable, and contains the Node.js runtime needed for the app.

---

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments` – whatever you prefer) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use a different registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> *What this does:*  
> The Deployment runs 2 replicas of the container.  
> The Service exposes the app on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you want external access).

---

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t already exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (needed for multi‑arch builds)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - name: Login to DockerHub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password)  
> (If you’re using another registry, adjust the login step accordingly.)

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Dockerfile** in the repo root.  
* A `k8s/` folder containing `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.  
* A `.github/workflows/ci.yml` that triggers on pushes to `main`.  
* In the Actions tab of GitHub, a successful run that builds and pushes the Docker image.

That’s it! 🎉 If you want to deploy the app to a cluster right away, you can run:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

(Assuming you have `kubectl` configured to talk to your cluster.)
